blurb.en: Say hello the local way, greet elders first, and close a talk politely.
Keep any conversation alive when you don't understand yet.
Answer the first questions everyone asks: name, home, work, family.
Ask prices, bargain fairly, count, pay and get change.
Agree a fare, give directions to a driver and get off where you want.
Get help fast, and handle the pharmacy and the doctor.
Order, say how you like it, and be a good guest at someone's table.
Visit a family home, honour the elders, and leave well.
Make a plan on the phone: when, where, and 'I'll call you back'.
Say how you are, talk about the day, and react like a friend.

sw.note: The reply is Sijambo (I'm well). To an elder say Shikamoo instead (st-0041). To a group: Hamjambo? 'Jambo' alone is what tourists hear; Kenyans say Hujambo or Habari.
To a group: Habari zenu? Greet an elder with Shikamoo first.

en.text: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

sw.note: First sentence reuses reviewed amb-0012 exactly.
To a group: Asanteni.
Sijaelewa = I haven't understood (yet). Both are said every day.
Adapted from reviewed amb-0027 (Tafadhali sema tena pole pole).
Pole pole = slowly. (Pole alone = sorry for your trouble.)
Na- is the everyday short form of nina- (I am ...ing).
Kuongea is everyday Kenyan; kuzungumza is the more formal word for 'speak'.
Adapted from reviewed amb-0981 (Neno hilo lina maana gani?).

en.text: How do you say this in Kiswahili?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0980 exactly. Literally 'this, in Kiswahili, is called how?'.
Many requests start with Naomba (I ask for) instead: Naomba maji. Use one or the other, not both.
Also used to say sorry. Add a title to be warm: Samahani, mama. / Samahani, kaka.
Accepting something offered: naomba (I ask for it), not tafadhali.
Wording from reviewed amb-0065 (How much for this?).
Choo is class 7 (kiko). Choo iko wapi? is also heard; we teach the standard.
Naomba (I ask for) is the polite way to order anything.
No gender in Swahili: one form for everyone.
Swahili greetings are questions: 'news of the morning?'. The reply is Nzuri or Salama.
Alt is reviewed amb-0871.
To a group: Kwaherini.
Hakuna shida from reviewed amb-0254.
Umeshindaje = how did you spend the day? (reviewed amb-0007 uses it).
Wording from reviewed amb-0032. Lala salama = sleep well, said at bedtime.
Group greeting (ham- = you all). The reply is Hatujambo. Hamjambo wote? is also heard.
Reuses reviewed amb-0026 exactly.
Adapted from reviewed amb-0030 (Tutaonana baadaye leo).
Adapted from reviewed amb-0029 (Tutaonana kesho asubuhi).
Reuses reviewed amb-0031 exactly.
Same pattern as Uwe na siku njema (amb-0031).
Reuses reviewed amb-0301 (Thank you so much).
Reuses reviewed amb-0304 exactly. Karibu = the reply to asante.
Samahani = I apologise / excuse me. Pole = sorry for your trouble (someone trips, is sick, had a hard day).
Common on the coast and among Muslims. The Latin spelling of this Arabic greeting varies a lot.
The fixed reply. Spelling varies (Wa alaikum salaam).
Respect greeting from a younger person. The elder replies Marahaba. Mzee = respected elder (man); to a woman elder say mama (or bibi for a grandmother). This is a word swap, not grammar.

en.text: Fine. I slept well, thank you.

sw.note: Adapted: Swahili answers the morning greeting with Nzuri (good) instead of saying 'good morning' back.

en.text: Good morning! How did you sleep?

sw.note: Reuses reviewed amb-0004 exactly.
Hosts repeat karibu. To a group: Karibuni, karibuni. Ingieni ndani.
Reuses reviewed amb-0021 exactly: the set phrase for 'have a seat'. Keti is correct but sounds bookish in Kenya.
Tunamshukuru Mungu (we thank God) is the everyday set phrase, even about yourself.
Nimeelewa = I've got it (now).

en.text: Can you write it for me?

sw.note: ku-ni-andiki-a = to write for me.
Nimetamka = did I pronounce it.
Alt = correct me when I get it wrong.

en.text: Speak to me in Kiswahili, please.

sw.note: Subira (patience) is the coastal favourite; uvumilivu is heard everywhere.
Umekaribia = you've come close (almost right).

A man says nimeoa (I have married); a woman says nimeolewa (I have been married). Pattern of reviewed amb-0194. The alt Nina mke is a man's line; a woman says Nina mume.
Reviewed amb-0174 (What do you do for work?).

Hii fits most things (class 9). A ki- thing: hiki. An m- thing (mti): huu. A ji-/class 5 thing (tunda, embe): hili.

Reuses reviewed amb-0139 exactly. Most people just say M-Pesa.
Said while handing over money or a thing.
Reuses reviewed amb-0099 exactly (reviewed at medium confidence).
The Kenyan notes are fifty, one hundred, two hundred, five hundred and one thousand shillings.
Adapted: a vegetable seller (mama mboga) says 'what shall I give you?'.

Plural: shouted to everyone around.

Wording of reviewed amb-0880 (Where is the chemist?). Kenyans call a pharmacy a kemisti.

sw.note: Say the dose back to check you heard it.
Mzio is the standard word; aleji is what many Kenyans say. Swap in your real allergy, or skip.
Literally 'I have been stolen-from my bag'. Begi langu (class 5) is standard; begi yangu is also heard.
Adapted: the chemist asks 'what can I help you with?'.

Kenyan chai comes with milk and sugar already in.
Black tea is chai ya rangi.

Pilipili = chilli.
Adapted: accepting an invitation, Swahili says 'I will come'. After Karibu tena (come again): nitakuja tena or nitarudi.

Respect: greet with Shikamoo first. Mzee = elder (man); to a woman elder say mama. A word swap, not grammar.

Reuses reviewed amb-0034 (Say hello to your family for me), same meaning.

From reviewed amb-0041 (Niko njiani, nitafika punde).

(Called at the door: may I come in?)

blurb.en: The first talk of the day at the gate, with an older neighbour: respect greeting first, then the long morning greetings nobody skips.
An open-air vegetable stall run by a mama mboga: prices per kilo or per pile, bargaining is normal, M-Pesa is taken.
A motorbike taxi (bodaboda) from the stage: agree the fare first, guide the rider with left, right and landmarks, pay cash or M-Pesa.
Tea at a small hoteli or in a home: chai is boiled with milk and sugar; on the coast, street sellers pour tiny cups of kahawa in the evening.
The neighbourhood chemist (kemisti or duka la dawa): the pharmacist advises on the spot and tells you the dose in words.
A weekend visit to a family home: call Hodi at the door, greet every elder first, eat what is offered, leave with blessings.
A quick call to make a plan: who you are, when, where, and a bad network.
The office morning: greet everyone one by one, the ten o'clock chai round, a meeting at saa nne, and goodbye in the evening.

meaning.en: Small steady efforts add up to something big.

proverbs.literal: little by little fills the measure

meaning.en: Rushing spoils the work. Slow down and it comes out right.
Steady and gentle is how you actually get there.

proverbs.literal: slowly slowly is the way to travel

meaning.en: Asking questions is not foolish; it is how you learn.
Ignore wise advice and you will get hurt.

proverbs.literal: one who won't listen to an elder breaks a leg

meaning.en: A guest coming is a blessing on the house.

proverbs.literal: let the guest come so the host may be relieved

meaning.en: Together you are strong. The full saying goes on: utengano ni udhaifu (division is weakness).
One person alone cannot do it; you need another hand.

proverbs.literal: one finger does not crush a louse

meaning.en: Fix the small problem now or rebuild the whole thing later.

proverbs.literal: if you don't seal the crack you will build a wall

meaning.en: Some things cannot be undone. Think before you act.

proverbs.literal: spilled water cannot be gathered up

proverbs.text: Asiyefunzwa na mamaye hufunzwa na ulimwengu.

meaning.en: If you won't be taught gently, life will teach you hard.

proverbs.literal: one not taught by their mother is taught by the world

meaning.en: What you promised, you owe. Keep your word.
